stories.topic: Cross-Checking the CPI: Hygiene as a Pre-condition
stories.summary: Years ago, working with Ila Patnaik, Ajay set out to test whether the Indian government's Consumer Price Index could be trusted. They used the CMIE household survey to derive an independent set of consumption weights and cross-checked them against the CPI's official weights, then used private-sector price data to test the CPI's prices. Both checked out. So while Indian government data should generally be viewed with great skepticism (and GDP data famously fails this test), the CPI passes the hygiene check.
stories.insight: Before applying any government statistic, do the hygiene work of independently verifying its foundations. State capability fails uniformly across domains, so a country whose policing and judiciary are weak will tend to have weak measurement too. The exceptions are precious and worth identifying empirically rather than assuming.

stories.summary: As far back as 2002, Ajay was talking with Finance Minister Yashwant Sinha about inflation targeting. Sinha's response was that the idea was too far ahead of the Indian intellectual mainstream — it had to be normalised in the wider intellectual debate before any future finance minister could implement it. Ajay took that as wise counsel about how reform actually moves.
stories.insight: Big policy ideas rarely fail on technical merits — they fail when the surrounding intellectual climate isn't ready. The work of reform is partly the work of patiently cultivating that climate, and accepting that a decade of conversation might be necessary scaffolding for a single law.

stories.topic: The Ways and Means Agreement: A Contract Stands In Where Law Cannot
stories.summary: In the 1990s, when the parliament couldn't be made to pass a law shutting down RBI's automatic monetisation of government deficits, Montek Ahluwalia and C. Rangarajan instead signed a public contract — the Ways and Means Agreement — where the Ministry of Finance promised never to ask, and RBI promised never to give. That public ceremony was a milestone in Indian monetary policy and freed RBI of one of its worst distortions.
stories.insight: When the legislative path is blocked, a binding public agreement between principals can do remarkable work. The trick was the people: it benefited from having two enlightened figures in the right chairs at the right time, which is the fragile lottery on which a lot of institutional progress quietly rides.

stories.summary: Inflation targeting in advanced economies anchors at 2%. India chose 4% with a band of 2-6%. Ajay walks through the reasoning: 2% is perilously close to zero so leaves no headroom for rate cuts in a deep crisis (you can only cut to zero); India's broken financial system muffles monetary transmission, so a higher policy rate is needed to get any work done; and that same poor transmission makes a precise point target unreasonable, so a band gives the central bank realistic room. The plan was to tighten the band over time as the financial system improved.
stories.insight: Good institutional design doesn't copy the answers of advanced economies — it understands why those answers work there and engineers a different one that fits the local plumbing. The 4 percent plus-minus-two number is itself a piece of careful economic design.

stories.topic: FSLRC and the Draft Indian Financial Code
stories.summary: In 2011 Justice Srikrishna led the Financial Sector Legislative Reforms Commission, with Ajay and Ila Patnaik leading a 35-person research team at NIPFP — a rare government commission backed by genuine technical capability. The mandate was to zero-base 60-odd messy old laws and replace them with one clean Indian Financial Code, with chapters on RBI, inflation targeting, and the monetary policy committee. The first draft came out in 2013.
stories.insight: Government commissions usually fail because they have neither time nor technical muscle. FSLRC succeeded as an architectural exercise because it had both — and because it imagined the financial state from first principles rather than patching the existing chaos.

stories.topic: Chidambaram's Note: 'I Leave This to My Successor'
stories.summary: By the end of 2013 / early 2014, the Monetary Policy Framework Agreement was drafted, with input from Ajay's team, KP Krishnan, Chidambaram, Montek Ahluwalia and Manmohan Singh. Chidambaram, knowing his government was a lame duck, wrote on the file that this was one of the most important milestones in Indian history and should not be done lightly by an outgoing government — he would leave it to his successor.
stories.insight: Statesmanship is partly the discipline of refusing to do the right thing at the wrong time. Chidambaram's deferral preserved the legitimacy of a reform that would otherwise have been rolled back by a hostile incoming government.

stories.summary: Retelling the story KP Krishnan told him in their 8-hour Seen and the Unseen episode: Krishnan briefs new Finance Minister Arun Jaitley on the Monetary Policy Framework Agreement; the next morning Jaitley calls and says yes, let's do it. Krishnan is alarmed — this is far-reaching, has Jaitley actually read it? Jaitley, slightly irritated, says: if the country's finest economic mind (Manmohan Singh) and finest legal mind (Chidambaram) have said this must be done, who am I to ask? Amit notes wistfully that this kind of grace 'never happens again' — Indian politics has changed.
stories.insight: Trust in expertise across party lines is itself a form of institutional capital, and it can vanish silently. A reform that took fifteen years of work cleared its final hurdle because of a single politician's humility about his own competence — a humility that is now in short supply.

stories.topic: The 'Temporary Measure' Erased From the RBI Act
stories.summary: When the British wrote the RBI Act in 1934, the preamble said that because the international monetary system was disorganised, India's monetary system could not yet be determined — so the RBI was being created 'as a temporary measure.' Those words sat in the preamble for over eighty years. In 2016, when the act was amended to formalise inflation targeting, that text was finally replaced with 'in order to deliver price stability.'
stories.insight: An institution can stand for eighty years with 'temporary' written on its forehead. A law's preamble matters because purpose matters; only in 2016 did the RBI finally get a proper one. Indian institutions are still discovering what they are for.

recommendations.context: A meta-recommendation Amit makes after the inflation-targeting story.
recommendations.reason: Inflation targeting is a rare elegant piece of legislation but it is always under threat. The price of preserving good policy is constant vigilance — refusing to take any settled good for granted.

recommendations.creator: Joni Mitchell
recommendations.reason: Mitchell is a genuine pioneer — singer-songwriter and masterful instrumentalist whose guitar and piano playing are extraordinary, and whose work was admired across folk, rock, and jazz (collaborations with Mingus and Pastorius). Blue is Amit's favourite album of hers; best heard with headphones on a quiet day, alone.

recommendations.item: The Economic Consequences of the Peace
recommendations.creator: John Maynard Keynes
recommendations.context: Linked in show notes; cited as Keynes's pamphlet on the post-WWI reparations.
recommendations.reason: Keynes argued that the impossibly high reparations imposed on Germany would force it to print money and trigger hyperinflation — and helped seed the demand for something resembling GDP, on the principle that you cannot make sane demands of a national economy you cannot measure.

recommendations.item: Demystifying GDP (Episode 130, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Rajeswari Sengupta
recommendations.context: Linked when Amit references the larger story of how GDP came to exist.
recommendations.reason: The deep-dive on what GDP actually is, why it was invented, and how it is measured — context for the present episode's claim that you cannot reason about an economy you cannot measure.

recommendations.creator: Centre for Monitoring Indian Economy
recommendations.context: Linked in show notes; the survey Ajay used to cross-check the CPI weights.
recommendations.reason: A vast survey of around 190,000 households, three times a year, across about 90 elements of household consumption — independent enough of government measurement to serve as a check on it.

recommendations.creator: Milton Friedman
recommendations.context: Friedman's 1968 AEA presidential address; linked in show notes.
recommendations.reason: The source of the deep insight that high inflation interferes with the information-processing of firms — they cannot tell whether a price change is a real signal about the economy or just monetary noise. The intellectual foundation of the case for price stability.

recommendations.item: The Use of Knowledge in Society
recommendations.creator: Friedrich Hayek
recommendations.context: Linked in show notes; the philosophical underlay for the price-system arguments in the episode.
recommendations.reason: Hayek's classic on prices as the mechanism by which decentralised knowledge is aggregated into resource allocation. Without it, the case for low inflation as protection of the price system has no foundation.

recommendations.item: Why Is Solving India's Inflation Crisis Important? (2012)
recommendations.creator: Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Linked in show notes; Ajay's contemporaneous case for inflation targeting in India.
recommendations.reason: An early formulation of the arguments developed in this episode, written during the 2007-onwards inflation crisis that ultimately won the case for institutional reform.

recommendations.creator: Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Linked in show notes; Ajay's design paper from the period when the MPC was being built.
recommendations.reason: The technical companion to the political story told in the episode — what an inflation-targeting MPC should look like, written as the Indian one was being designed.

recommendations.creator: Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Linked in show notes; Ajay's column on monetary policy.
recommendations.reason: Ajay's argument on what is lost when the central bank's shock-absorber function is impaired — relevant to the engine-room mechanics of monetary policy described in the episode.

recommendations.item: How to Do Development (Episode 57, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Linked when growth as the 'highest god' is invoked.
recommendations.reason: The companion episode in which Amit and Ajay argue at length for growth as India's central moral imperative for poverty alleviation — the foundation of why inflation matters.

recommendations.item: Public Choice Theory Explains SO MUCH (Episode 33, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay tells the gentle reader to go look at this when explaining why central banks need accountability.
recommendations.reason: The episode that lays out public choice theory — the intellectual framework that says even appointed central bankers will pursue private objectives unless held accountable, and so should not be granted unchecked power.

recommendations.item: The Long Road to Change (Episode 36, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Amit references this when Ajay narrates the multi-decade journey of inflation targeting in India.
recommendations.reason: The companion episode on how policy reforms slowly travel through the Indian pipeline — useful context for why an idea pitched in 2002 took until 2016 to become law.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with KP Krishnan

recommendations.reason: The original source for the story of Arun Jaitley's overnight 'yes' to the Monetary Policy Framework Agreement, and a deep dive into how a generation of Indian reformers actually got things done.

recommendations.context: Linked in show notes alongside the reform-history references.
recommendations.reason: The episode on the Indian reform tradition out of which figures like Rangarajan, Tarapore, Ahluwalia and Chidambaram emerged — the human substrate of the inflation-targeting story.

core_ideas.concept: Inflation Is Always and Everywhere a Monetary Phenomenon
core_ideas.explanation: Localised price changes happen all the time because of supply and demand shocks (an apple orchard hit by maggots). Inflation, properly defined, is the broad rise in all prices — and that happens because the quantity of money has changed relative to goods and services. Modern central banks no longer literally print money, but by setting the short-term interest rate they expand and contract the money base. Whoever controls money causes inflation.
core_ideas.quote: Inflation is always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon. — Milton Friedman

core_ideas.concept: Inflation Is a Tax on the Poor
core_ideas.explanation: When new money enters the economy, it doesn't get distributed in proportion to existing holdings — those closest to the printing press benefit first, before prices adjust. The poor, with little capacity to hedge or adjust, are the greatest sufferers. So unchecked inflation is a regressive transfer of wealth from poor to rich, and any government that allows it must be held accountable.
core_ideas.quote: Inflation is a tax on the poor.

core_ideas.concept: High Inflation Corrupts the Information-Processing of Firms
core_ideas.explanation: The deep Friedmanite insight from the 1968 paper. The price system is how decentralised knowledge gets aggregated into resource allocation; firms read price signals to decide what to make and where to invest. When inflation is high it is also variable, and the cross-sectional dispersion of prices grows. Firms can no longer tell whether a price rise reflects scarcity or genuine demand or simply monetary noise. They make wrong adjustments, misallocate resources, and growth suffers. So low and stable inflation is a precondition for the price system to work at all.
core_ideas.quote: High inflation messes with the information processing problem of firms.

core_ideas.explanation: Every firm has a bounded budget of cognitive and contracting capacity to respond to a changing world. Real change — technology, tastes, factor costs — is exhausting enough; firms have to reorganise factories, hire and fire, renegotiate contracts. Inflation is acid dripping on every nominal contract: parties get pulled back into renegotiations not because the real economy changed but because the unit of account did. This is depreciation of contracts — running to stand still — and it consumes precious adjustment capacity that should have gone to real economic improvement.

Long-term plans — building a highway, taking a 30-year mortgage, designing a multi-decade business — require stable expectations about interest rates and nominal contracts. Under high and variable inflation, those expectations evaporate and planning collapses to the present. The country's planning horizon shrinks; complex multi-year projects don't get built. Growth depends on long horizons, so stable inflation is structural infrastructure for growth itself.

The position of modern monetary economics: the highest contribution a central bank can make to society is to deliver low and stable inflation, and nothing else. Pursuing other objectives (managing the exchange rate, propping up growth, intervening in equity markets) inevitably comes at the cost of price stability. The central bank should be like a dentist — narrow, accountable, technical — not a high priest of the economy. One job. One lever. One target.
core_ideas.quote: If central bankers would be humble like dentists, that would be a pretty fine thing.

core_ideas.concept: Power Must Be Matched by Accountability (Public Choice Applied)
core_ideas.explanation: A foundational principle of public administration: every grant of state power must be paired with an accountability mechanism. Central banks have the extraordinary power of creating fiat money; without an external accountability frame, they will fail (and have, repeatedly, for centuries). Inflation targeting is precisely such a frame. The 1987 New Zealand innovation was simple agency theory — pay the central bank governor a bonus if she hits the target. This refused the romantic idea of an untouchable expert priesthood and treated the central bank like any other agency.

core_ideas.concept: Inflation Targeting Threads the Independence Needle
core_ideas.explanation: There are two failure modes for a central bank. One: it is controlled by the government, which uses it for election business cycles — keeping rates low in the year before an election to engineer feel-good growth and inflate the incumbent's vote. Two: it claims lofty independence and acts on whim, captured by special interests or by economists' self-image as 'good guys' immune to public choice. Inflation targeting is the elegant middle path: define the role narrowly, give operational independence to deliver it, and hold them accountable with a public target. No populism, no priesthood.
core_ideas.quote: Everybody else we do public choice theory. But for us, we are good guys and we should be given a free hand. Nah, that's not how this works.

core_ideas.concept: Inside the Engine Room: One Lever, A Slow Steering Wheel
core_ideas.explanation: Good central banks tinker with exactly one price — the short-term interest rate — and leave everything else (long bond yields, exchange rates, equity prices) to markets. The trouble is the long lag: changes to the short rate take time to work through the economy, like a car whose wheel responds only after a delay. The central bank must therefore forecast the future, not the present. In developing economies with bad models, that's hard, so India uses a band rather than a point target.

core_ideas.concept: India's 4 Percent (Plus-or-Minus 2) Was a Designed Number
core_ideas.explanation: The choice of 4% target with a 2-6% band was not arbitrary. (1) Two percent is too close to zero — leaves no headroom for rate cuts in a deep crisis since central banks can't go below zero meaningfully. (2) India's broken financial system muffles monetary transmission, so larger policy rate moves are needed to do real work, which requires a higher baseline. (3) That same poor transmission makes a precise 4.00 target unreasonable, so a band gives realistic room. The design also envisaged a glide path: as the financial system improved, the band would narrow.

core_ideas.concept: When Law Fails, Use a Public Contract
core_ideas.explanation: Twice in modern Indian monetary policy, a critical reform was achieved not by parliamentary law but by a binding public agreement between the Ministry of Finance and RBI: first the Ways and Means Agreement (Ahluwalia and Rangarajan signing the end of automatic deficit monetisation), and later the Monetary Policy Framework Agreement of February 2015 (Maharishi and Rajan signing the inflation target). These show a workable institutional pattern when legislative paths are blocked: a public ceremony, two principals, a written commitment. Fragile, dependent on the right people, but real.

Before treating any government statistic as truth, do an independent hygiene check. Ajay and Ila Patnaik did this for the Indian CPI: cross-checking weights against the CMIE survey and prices against private data. The CPI passed. The GDP famously hasn't. The general principle: a state with weak capability fails uniformly across domains, so don't single out the statisticians, but don't trust them blindly either. Measurement is the foundation; everything else falls if the foundation is rotten.

core_ideas.concept: WPI Is Not Wholesale, Not Meaningful, But Useful
core_ideas.explanation: A pro-tip from Ajay: the Wholesale Price Index has nothing wholesale about it (the name confuses everyone), is not a meaningful index because it represents nobody's actual consumption basket (it's 'random weights made up by some economists'), but is a useful long-run database of underlying component prices. So use the WPI's component series (e.g., the long history of nickel prices) as a database, never the aggregate WPI itself. Use the CPI as the inflation measure.

core_ideas.concept: Reform Moves at the Speed of the Surrounding Intellectual Climate
core_ideas.explanation: Yashwant Sinha's wisdom to Ajay in 2002: an idea has to become normalised in the wider intellectual debate before any future minister can do it. The case for inflation targeting was pitched in 2002, refined through FSLRC in 2011-2013, made urgent by the 2007-onwards inflation crisis that discredited the old RBI, drafted into a Monetary Policy Framework Agreement, deferred by Chidambaram, signed by Jaitley in 2015, and codified into law in 2016. The lesson: institutional reform is patient horticulture, not revolution. The intellectual ground has to be prepared for years before any single bill can land.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Ajay imagines Amit's personalised inflation index: 'Vast amounts of bacon, tiny amounts of bread… Amit Bhai is a good devout non-vegetarian and he eats bacon as a matter of principle.'

Amit interrupts Ajay's hypothetical of a self-employed doctor charging more under inflation: 'Except some of your patients die because food is so expensive they can't afford it anymore and then you have less patients.' Ajay almost answers seriously about inflation shocks and infant mortality before catching the joke.
Ajay's three-part jab at the WPI: 'The wholesale price index is basically not wholesale, not an index, and not a price.'

Amit's hypothetical contract for the show: 'Rupees one million will be paid per podcast to the great podcaster.' Then breaking the fourth wall: 'I just want to tell dear listeners we are not getting any money for this. It's a labour of love.'
Ajay's image for inflation eroding nominal contracts: 'High and variable inflation is the acid that drips on these contracts and destroys their meaning.'
Ajay imagining the renegotiation pressure: 'See Mr Beer Biceps, he gets paid so much better than me and I'm not being paid well.'
Amit on Ajay's word choice: 'I love the way you use phrases central bank and penitent in the same sentence. It reminds me of the famous song Please Forgive Me, no matter what I do.'
Amit's request to gentle readers: list every musical reference in the comments. 'If you don't do that, I will be unsatisfied.'

Ajay's affectionate description of the boom years: 'Oh ye young readers of Everything is Everything, if you haven't lived in the glory years of 2007 and 1997, you have no idea what economic success looks like. You have just lived in some grim dark days and you have normalised the sadness of what it means to be the Indian economy.'
Ajay at the end of the episode: 'Out of talking about all this, my CPU power has dwindled away. Now I'm a Z80.'

Amit on growth as the highest god: 'You say the highest god, you know it is almost as if gods are standing in a tier of the city. The Chotu gods and there are higher gods.' Ajay agrees they had to climb the mountains of beer (referring to the Development episode) to talk about a highest god.

Ajay's metaphor for the 1934 RBI Act: 'It's like there was a child who was a full grown man standing in 2015 but on his forehead was the word: you're a temporary measure because we haven't yet figured out what to do.'
Milton Friedman: 'Inflation is always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon' — the load-bearing slogan of the entire episode.
Keynes (paraphrased): 'If economists were humble like dentists, that would be a pretty fine thing' — invoked by Ajay to describe what a central banker should aspire to be.

Montagu Norman, longtime Bank of England governor: 'I don't have reasons, I have my instincts' — Ajay invokes him as the archetype of the unaccountable central banker who claims a mystique above public choice theory.
Knut Wicksell — 'modern central banks, we are all Wicksellian now,' meaning the policy instrument is the short-term interest rate, not the money supply directly.

Weimar hyperinflation: 'What you could buy a house with is what you would need to buy a loaf of bread a week later' — the canonical example of monetary collapse, leading to the rise of Adolf Hitler and Keynes's pamphlet The Economic Consequences of the Peace.

1987 New Zealand: the birthplace of inflation targeting and the bonus-for-the-governor mechanism, the first time after centuries of central-banking failure that the institution started actually working.
20 February 2015: the date Rajiv Mehrishi and Raghuram Rajan signed India's Monetary Policy Framework Agreement — Ajay regrets it wasn't done as a public ceremony.
